candidates.title: Scale-sensitivity of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for LLM-driven network-configuration repair
candidates.research_question: Does a generate–verify–repair pipeline materially reduce incorrect or unsafe configuration repairs compared to raw LLM outputs as network topology size and heterogeneity increase?
hypotheses: H1: GVR produces a higher proportion of syntactically and semantically correct repairs than raw LLM outputs (directional, testable).
H2: The relative benefit of GVR over raw LLM decreases as topology size and cross-vendor heterogeneity grow (interaction effect).
candidates.proposed_design: Controlled, paired experiment using a corpus of repair tasks derived from Cornetto-style scenarios plus additional larger synthetic topologies. For each task: (a) prompt a single hosted LLM to produce a repair (raw), (b) run same LLM within a GVR loop where a deterministic verifier checks syntax/route/policy constraints and requests up to N repairs, (c) record final accepted patch. Validators implemented as deterministic config parsers and reachability/policy checks in simulation. Use fixed seeds; preregister N, retry policy, and topology-size bins (small/medium/large).
candidates.expected_data: Per-task: raw output, GVR output(s), verifier pass/fail logs, number of repair iterations, validator-detected regressions, execution time, and binary correctness labels from deterministic checks.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in proportion-correct (validator-passed without regressions) between GVR and raw LLM, stratified by topology-size bin.
candidates.analysis_outline: Paired proportion tests (McNemar or paired bootstrap) for primary outcome; logistic regression to test interaction between method (GVR/raw) and topology size/heterogeneity; report effect sizes with 95% CIs; failure-mode taxonomy and case examples.
risks: Deterministic verifier may not capture all operational correctness criteria (construct validity).
API rate limits or cost could constrain iterations (infrastructure).
If verifier is too strict, useful fixes may be rejected (false negatives).

candidates.title: Comparative evaluation of orchestration styles for LLM-based repair: single-pass, iterative-tool, and multi-agent
candidates.research_question: Which orchestration style for LLM-driven repair minimizes regressions and repair churn on common NetOps repair tasks?
hypotheses: H1: Iterative-tool orchestration (LLM + verifier/tool loop) yields fewer regressions than single-pass generation.
H2: A lightweight multi-agent orchestration yields marginal improvement over iterative-tool at higher compute cost (testable difference in regression rates and cost).
candidates.proposed_design: Implement three orchestration strategies using the same hosted LLM(s): (A) single-pass: one-shot repair; (B) iterative-tool: LLM + deterministic verifier with up to M iterations and explicit repair prompts; (C) multi-agent: split roles (proposer, critic, synthesizer) using separate prompt templates and limited message exchange. Evaluate on the same benchmark task set (Cornetto + expanded scenarios). Measure correctness, regression rate, iterations, wall time, and API calls. Predefine orchestration protocols and limits in preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task outputs from each orchestration, verifier logs, inter-agent messages (for (C)), iteration counts, cost (model calls), and binary/graded correctness and regression indicators.
candidates.primary_outcome: Regression rate (proportion of repairs introducing a new violation) for each orchestration style; pairwise comparisons with cost-normalized metrics.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare proportions with pairwise tests and adjust for multiple comparisons; cost-effectiveness curves (regression-rate vs model-calls); qualitative analysis of representative failure modes per orchestration.
risks: High model-call budget required for multi-agent runs; may approach API limits.
Orchestration templates (prompts) may be sensitive; prompt-sensitivity threatens internal validity.
Correlated error modes across agents could negate ensemble benefits.

candidates.title: Assessing LLM self-reported/calibrated confidence as an automated gate for NetOps actions
candidates.research_question: Can LLM-internal or proxy confidence signals be calibrated to reliably gate automatic application of suggested NetOps repairs without external deterministic verification?
hypotheses: H1: Raw LLM self-reported confidence (or single-response heuristic) is poorly calibrated for correctness on repair tasks.
H2: Post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling, ensemble disagreement) improves calibration but remains insufficient alone for high-assurance gating at typical operational thresholds.
H3: Combining calibrated confidence with lightweight syntactic checks yields acceptable operational trade-offs (testable).
candidates.proposed_design: Collect LLM repairs plus any available token/log-prob proxies or use Monte Carlo sampling to estimate uncertainty. Compute calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score) against deterministic correctness labels. Apply calibration methods (temperature scaling, Platt) and alternative proxies (ensemble/response-variance). Evaluate gating performance by plotting ROC/precision-recall for different thresholds and compare to verifier-based gating baseline.
candidates.expected_data: Raw responses, per-response confidence proxy scores, calibrated scores, correctness labels, calibration curves, and gating-operating-point metrics (false-accept rate, false-reject rate).
candidates.primary_outcome: Calibration effectiveness measured by reduction in ECE and operational gating performance (false-accept rate at target true-accept rate) relative to verifier baseline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute calibration metrics and confidence-utility curves; compare gating trade-offs with verifier baseline; statistical tests on ECE reductions; sensitivity analysis across task difficulty and topology size.
risks: Some hosted LLM APIs do not expose reliable logits or probability outputs; Monte Carlo proxies increase model-call cost.
Calibration on synthetic benchmarks may not generalize to production distributions.
Operational thresholds are subjective and domain-dependent.

candidates.title: Impact of semantic tracing and human-review gating on repair safety and time-to-fix
candidates.research_question: Does integrating semantic tracing (structured justification and provenance) plus a simulated human-review gate reduce regression incidence and time-to-fix compared to ungated automated repair?
hypotheses: H1: Repairs accompanied by machine-generated semantic traces increase detectability of risky edits and reduce regression incidence after a single human-review pass.
H2: Semantic traces reduce average reviewer triage time compared to presenting raw diffs (measurable in simulated human-review latency).
candidates.proposed_design: Instrument LLM repair outputs to include structured semantic traces (intent, affected objects, risk tags). Simulate a human-reviewer using a deterministic heuristic model that uses traces to accept/reject with bounded time cost; compare to baseline where reviewer sees raw diff and runs same heuristic with longer expected evaluation time. Evaluate regression rates, number of false-rejections/false-accepts, and simulated time-to-approve across tasks from Cornetto and extended scenarios.
candidates.expected_data: Repair proposals with traces, reviewer decisions and latencies (simulated), final applied repairs, regression indicators, and counts of manual interventions or rollbacks.
candidates.primary_outcome: Regression incidence post-review and median simulated review time per accepted repair between trace-assisted and raw-diff conditions.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare regression rates (proportions) and review-time distributions (nonparametric tests); sensitivity analysis on reviewer heuristic strictness; qualitative examples of trace utility/failure.
risks: Simulated reviewer heuristics may not reflect real operator behavior (external validity).
Semantic-trace generation quality depends on prompt design (prompt sensitivity).

candidates.title: Ensemble voting of multiple LLMs for configuration repair: does ensemble reduce regressions vs single-model repairs?
candidates.research_question: Does majority-vote ensemble of multiple LLMs reduce the incidence of regressions and increase repair correctness compared to a single-model baseline on NetOps repair tasks?
hypotheses: H1: Ensembles of diverse LLMs produce fewer regressions than the best single model in the ensemble (tested across tasks).
H2: Correlated failure modes reduce ensemble gains on certain classes of tasks (testable via subgroup analysis).
candidates.proposed_design: Select 2–3 hosted LLMs (subject to API availability) and produce independent repairs per task. Use deterministic merging (majority vote on line-level edits or semantic-merge rules) to produce ensemble repair; compare against each single-model repair. Validate with deterministic verifier and record regressions, correctness, and model-call cost. Predefine merging rules and tie-breaking in preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per-model outputs, merged ensemble output, verifier results, regression labels, merged vs single-model correctness, and model-call counts.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in regression rate and correctness between ensemble output and the single best model, with cost-normalized comparison.
candidates.analysis_outline: Paired comparisons across tasks; subgroup analysis by task type; measure ensemble improvement vs cost (model-calls). Report examples where correlated errors nullify ensemble benefits.
risks: API cost and rate limits when calling multiple models may be prohibitive.
Models may exhibit correlated hallucinations reducing ensemble advantage.
